title: The Body Keeps the Score
author: Bessel van der Kolk
thesisParagraph: Traumatic stress is not only a memory problem; it changes arousal, perception, attachment, bodily awareness, and the capacity for choice. Durable recovery requires restoring safety, agency, integration, and connection through methods that engage body, brain, language, relationships, and community.

signatureMoves: opens clinical mechanisms through patient histories, bodily sensation, and trauma physiology
names brain regions, attachment, memory, and treatment modalities without losing lived experience
moves between individual suffering and institutional or public-health consequences
keeps returning from diagnosis to safety, agency, body, and relationship
mixes clinical case histories with research milestones and personal professional history
avoidMoves: Avoid "The point is" as a paragraph hinge.
Avoid "the question is" as a setup crutch.
Avoid triadic abstract-noun lists such as clarity, courage, and resilience.
Do not present trauma as a purely cognitive misunderstanding.
Do not treat medication or talk therapy as universal solutions.

voiceSpecimens: The symptom is not merely a thought; it is a body preparing for danger.
Recovery begins when safety becomes more than an idea.
teachingArc: The opening movement traces trauma from clinical discovery to brain imaging, showing why symptoms cannot be reduced to weak character or poor insight. The middle movement maps survival physiology, attachment, childhood trauma, diagnosis, and traumatic memory so the reader sees how disrupted safety becomes biology, relationships, and public health. The final movement turns toward recovery, moving from self-ownership and language through EMDR, yoga, IFS, PBSP structures, neurofeedback, and theater as different routes toward integration.
forbiddenMoves: Do not use trauma language as metaphor.
Do not detach symptoms from bodies, relationships, and safety.
